title: The Promotion Case
subtitle: Build the case, pitch it, and handle the answer
description: You have been in your role for two years. You believe you are ready for the next level. Over five scenes you will gather evidence, pitch your manager, handle pushback, wait through the uncertainty, and face the outcome.
learning_objectives: Build a data-backed promotion case rather than relying on tenure alone
Handle rejection or deferral with strategic thinking rather than emotional reactivity
Understand how managers evaluate readiness beyond performance metrics
reflection_prompt: What would you do differently in gathering evidence for your own promotion case?

scenes.title: Gathering the Evidence
scenes.narration: Priya, your skip-level manager, mentioned at the all-hands that promotion decisions happen in six weeks. You have a month to build your case. Your first instinct: write down everything you have done. But everyone does that.

choices.label: Document your last 12 months: projects, metrics, impact
Ask three colleagues to give you written impact feedback before building the case
Ask your manager what the bar for the next level actually looks like

scenes.narrative: Priya, your skip-level manager, mentioned at the all-hands that promotion decisions happen in six weeks. You have a month to build your case. Your first instinct: write down everything you have done. But everyone does that.

scenes.narration: You have a solid document: shipped features, metrics improved, projects led. It is factually accurate but reads like a job description. Something is missing.

choices.label: Add a section on scope: decisions you made, not just tasks you completed
Send it as-is — your record speaks for itself

scenes.narrative: You have a solid document: shipped features, metrics improved, projects led. It is factually accurate but reads like a job description. Something is missing.

scenes.narration: The feedback comes back with a pattern you did not expect: everyone mentions that you unblock others. That is not in any of your own notes.

choices.label: Build the case around cross-functional impact — not just your own work
Include the feedback but still lead with your individual output

scenes.narrative: The feedback comes back with a pattern you did not expect: everyone mentions that you unblock others. That is not in any of your own notes.

scenes.narration: Your manager says the bar for the next level is 'operating in ambiguity without hand-holding and multiplying the team.' You realise your evidence needs to show both, not just output.

choices.label: Rebuild the case to show ambiguity navigation and team multiplication specifically
Keep your existing evidence and add one example of each

scenes.narrative: Your manager says the bar for the next level is 'operating in ambiguity without hand-holding and multiplying the team.' You realise your evidence needs to show both, not just output.

scenes.narration: The conversation with your manager goes well. She asks hard questions. You answer most of them. At the end she says: 'I am going to bring this forward. I cannot promise, but the case is strong.'

choices.label: Thank her and ask what gaps she thinks the committee might flag
Thank her and wait for the decision

scenes.narrative: The conversation with your manager goes well. She asks hard questions. You answer most of them. At the end she says: 'I am going to bring this forward. I cannot promise, but the case is strong.'

scenes.narration: Your manager listens carefully. At the end she says: 'I want to support you but the committee needs more evidence of the next-level behaviours. Can you strengthen the case before I bring it forward?'

choices.label: Ask her to be specific: what exactly is the gap?
Feel deflated and say you will think about it

scenes.narrative: Your manager listens carefully. At the end she says: 'I want to support you but the committee needs more evidence of the next-level behaviours. Can you strengthen the case before I bring it forward?'

scenes.narration: You have a clear view of what the committee is looking for. The three weeks of waiting are hard but not anxious — you know the variables.

choices.label: Stay focused on current work — perform at the level you want, not the level you are at
Check in with your manager weekly to see if there is any news

scenes.narrative: You have a clear view of what the committee is looking for. The three weeks of waiting are hard but not anxious — you know the variables.

scenes.narration: The three weeks are difficult. You find yourself distracted, over-reading every message from your manager as a signal.

choices.label: Ask for a quick check-in just to understand where things stand
Wait it out — the decision is made now anyway

scenes.narrative: The three weeks are difficult. You find yourself distracted, over-reading every message from your manager as a signal.

scenes.narration: Your manager calls: 'The committee approved it. You are being promoted effective next quarter.' She adds: 'The cross-functional impact evidence was what made the difference.'
scenes.outcome_summary: You built the right case for the right audience. The promotion was earned twice — once in the work, once in how you articulated it.
scenes.narrative: Your manager calls: 'The committee approved it. You are being promoted effective next quarter.' She adds: 'The cross-functional impact evidence was what made the difference.'

scenes.narration: Your manager calls: 'You were approved for a lateral move to a higher-scope role. The committee felt you were ready for more responsibility but not quite at the next level yet. Give it one quarter.'
scenes.outcome_summary: A lateral to higher scope is not a consolation — it is the committee showing you the path. You are one strong quarter away.
scenes.narrative: Your manager calls: 'You were approved for a lateral move to a higher-scope role. The committee felt you were ready for more responsibility but not quite at the next level yet. Give it one quarter.'

scenes.narration: Your manager calls: 'The committee deferred. They want to see six more months. I know this is disappointing. Let us talk about what specifically they need to see.'
scenes.outcome_summary: Deferral is information, not rejection. The committee told you what the gap is. That is more valuable than silence. Start the next case today.
